weeks.title: A hundred is ten tens
weeks.objective: Build hundreds and explain trades without changing the amount.

connection.before: A ten is a bundle of ten ones.
connection.after: Hundreds, tens, and ones will name three-digit numbers.

days: Count ten bundles of ten with an adult.
Build three-digit amounts and name each piece.

Compare equal models and repair errors on B.

explanation: An adult can draw a small dot for one, a stick for ten, and a large square for one hundred. Count ten sticks together: 10, 20, 30, until 100. A hundred square stands for exactly the same quantity as those ten sticks; its drawing need not contain one hundred dots.

To build 243, place two hundred squares, four ten sticks, and three dots in labeled columns. Say the values, not just the digits: two hundreds is 200 and four tens is 40. Combine 200, 40, and 3 to name the whole collection.

Trading changes the arrangement, not the quantity. One hundred can become ten tens, and one ten can become ten ones. Have the child explain what was removed and what replaced it. Adding a new hundred while keeping all ten original tens would count the same amount twice.

explanation: Write the column names hundreds, tens, and ones above 358. Read the number as three hundred fifty-eight. Point to 3 and say 300, point to 5 and say 50, then point to 8 and say 8. These three values combine to make the numeral.

Expanded form shows the value held by each digit: 358 = 300 + 50 + 8. A zero holds an empty place. In 406 there are four hundreds, no tens, and six ones, so 400 + 6 is enough to show the values, but the numeral still needs its middle zero.

An adult may read number words aloud while the child builds or writes the numeral. Keep the spoken hundreds together before naming the remaining part. One thousand can be modeled as ten hundreds; it needs four digit places. Do not read 508 as fifty-eight, because its hundreds still count.

connection.before: Each digit has a value determined by its place.

explanation: Line up two three-digit numbers by place. Compare hundreds first because one extra hundred is larger than any possible difference in the tens and ones. For 521 and 498, five hundreds is more than four hundreds, so 521 is greater even though its other digits are smaller.

If the hundreds match, compare tens. If both hundreds and tens match, compare ones. Use a place-value drawing when the child is unsure. The symbols > and < show which side holds the greater amount; their open side faces the larger number. The symbol = means the quantities are the same.

Ask the child to finish the sentence, The first place that differs is ... . This keeps comparison tied to value instead of the size of the last digit. When ordering three numbers, choose the smallest first, then compare the two remaining amounts. Read the finished order aloud to check it.

weeks.title: Count by fives, tens, and hundreds
weeks.objective: Continue and explain skip-counts through 1000.

connection.before: Place-value comparisons identify increases.
connection.after: Skip-counting supports mental changes of ten and one hundred.

days: Move counters in equal groups of five.
Connect ten-jumps to place-value trades.
Complete forward counts on A.
Explain boundary crossings on B.
Apply skip-counts and check endpoints on C.
explanation: Begin a skip-count with an amount, then add the same amount every time. A count by fives from zero begins 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. An adult can move five counters into a growing pile for each spoken number so the child sees what each jump adds.

Counting by tens from 240 gives 250, 260, 270. The ones stay the same because only complete tens are added. At a boundary such as 290 to 300, ten tens trade for one hundred. A count by hundreds similarly adds one complete hundred each time, as long as the count stays within 1000.

Do not guess a pattern from the final digit alone: counts by five can end in 0 and 5, but each jump still needs to be five. Ask the child to name the jump and check two neighboring terms. Missing numbers can be found by going forward from a known number or backward from the next one.

weeks.title: Ten more and one hundred less
weeks.objective: Mentally add and subtract ten or one hundred with place-value reasoning.

connection.before: Skip-counts add equal groups.
connection.after: Place-value changes prepare regrouping in calculations.

days: Act out adding and removing bundles.
Practice tens changes across hundreds.

explanation: Ten more means adding one ten to the amount already there; ten less removes one ten. Begin with a drawing of 253. Adding a ten makes five tens become six, so the number is 263. The hundreds and ones stay the same in this example because no trade is needed.

When a place fills up or is empty, make a trade. Ten more than 293 is 303: nine tens plus one ten becomes a new hundred. Ten less than 402 is 392: exchange one hundred for ten tens before removing a ten. Keep the ones fixed during either change.

A change of one hundred usually changes the hundreds count while preserving the tens and ones. Ask the child to predict whether the answer should be greater or smaller before giving it. Check a mental change by reversing it; adding ten and then subtracting ten must return to the starting amount.

explanation: A number clue can describe its pieces, its position in order, or a change made to it. Read one clue at a time with an adult. For a number with six hundreds, two tens, and nine ones, start by building those values; do not try to guess from the sound of the whole number.

explanation: Use ten counters in a row and a second small group to make a ten visible. For 8 + 5, eight needs two more to reach ten. Split five into two and three, move two to the eight, and keep the remaining three: the total is thirteen. Nothing was added or lost during the move.

Doubles are another useful starting point. If the child knows 6 + 6 is 12, then 6 + 7 is one more, or 13. Ask which known fact helped and how the new fact differs. Brief, untimed practice should help the child remember sums of two one-digit numbers while retaining a way to reconstruct a forgotten fact.

Subtraction can undo addition. For 14 − 8, think eight and how many more make fourteen. Count two to reach ten, then four to reach fourteen; the missing part is six. Keep track of the amount added, not only the final landing. Encourage the child to check a difference by adding the removed part back.

days: Match labeled paper coins to values.

explanation: Use these United States coin values: a penny is 1 cent, a nickel 5 cents, a dime 10 cents, and a quarter 25 cents. An adult may label paper coin circles with these values. A coin’s value is not its size and is not always one cent; count value rather than the number of coins.

To count a mixed collection, begin with larger values and keep a running total. For one quarter, two dimes, and three pennies, say 25, 35, 45, 46, 47, 48 cents. Write 48¢, with the cent symbol after the number. Move or mark each coin as it is counted.

Different coin collections can have the same value. Ten pennies equal one dime, while two nickels also equal one dime. When making a value, state both the type and number of coins so the answer can be checked. This week uses whole cents up to 100; dollar-decimal notation is not needed.

weeks.title: Spend, save, and give change
weeks.objective: Solve whole-dollar and whole-cent money stories with correct notation.

connection.before: Coin values can be combined and compared.

days: Match the dollar and cent symbols to amounts.

explanation: Money problems need a clear unit. Write 36¢ for thirty-six cents and $8 for eight dollars. One dollar has the same value as 100 cents, but do not mix an unconverted dollar amount with a cent amount. This week separates whole-dollar purchases from cent purchases so every calculation uses matching units.

To find a purchase total, add the prices. To find change, subtract the cost from the payment, or count up from the cost to the payment. If two items are bought, first find their combined cost and only then find the change. Label that intermediate amount as cost, not change.

Use pretend bills or value-labeled coin circles with an adult. Ask whether the buyer has enough before calculating change. Check by joining the cost and change to recover the original payment. When more than one set of coins can make the answer, any set with the correct total is acceptable.

examples.prompt: A book costs $7 and a game costs $9. Pay with a $20 bill. Find the change.

weeks.title: Read clocks to five minutes
weeks.objective: Read and describe analog and digital times at five-minute marks.

connection.before: Skip-counting by five counts equal groups.
connection.after: Clock readings will be connected with a.m. and p.m. schedules.

days: Label five-minute counts around a drawn clock.
Move the hour hand gradually with an adult.

explanation: On an analog clock, the long minute hand counts minutes after the hour. Starting at 12 for zero minutes, count five minutes for each number: 1 means 5, 2 means 10, and so on to 11 meaning 55. One full turn returns to 12 at the next hour.

The short hour hand moves gradually. At 4:20 it is between 4 and 5, closer to 4; the minute hand points to 4. Read the hour already passed, not the next hour ahead. An adult can draw both hands and invite the child to describe which is long and which is short.

Digital time writes the hour, a colon, and two minute digits. Five minutes after eight is 8:05, not 8:5 or 8:50. For this week’s tasks all minute readings are multiples of five. When drawing, place the hour hand partway toward the next number rather than leaving it exactly on the earlier hour.

examples.prompt: The minute hand points to 7 and the hour hand is between 2 and 3. Read the time.

weeks.title: Tell when daily events happen
weeks.objective: Use five-minute clock readings and a.m./p.m. in daily schedules.

connection.before: Analog hands and digital labels show the same time.
connection.after: Number-line distances will connect with measurement.

days: Sort event cards into morning and after-noon groups.
Read noon and midnight labels explicitly.
Practice complete time labels on A.
Order times and explain missing context on B.
Read and discuss the supplied schedules on C.
explanation: A clock repeats its hour numbers twice in a day. The period from midnight up to noon is a.m.; from noon up to midnight is p.m. Breakfast at 7:30 in the morning is 7:30 a.m., while an evening event at 7:30 is 7:30 p.m. The clock hands alone cannot show which period is meant.

Read the event description together with the time. Noon is 12:00 p.m., and midnight is 12:00 a.m. To order events that all occur in one morning, compare the hours first and then the minutes. For events across the day, use the stated morning, afternoon, or evening context.

A schedule is a set of labels, not a requirement to calculate every duration. This week focuses on reading and ordering those labels. When a short five-minute change is given, use the next clock mark. Do not assume a later-looking hour number always happens later in the day; 1:00 p.m. follows 11:00 a.m.

weeks.objective: Choose length tools and read whole-unit ruler measurements.

connection.before: Equal units measure without gaps or overlaps.
connection.after: Different unit sizes will give different counts.

days: Inspect a ruler’s zero and unit label with an adult.
Count spaces rather than marks.
Read supplied ruler descriptions on A.
Diagnose placement and unit errors on B.
Choose tools and explain measurements on C.
explanation: Length tells how far one end of an object is from the other. A ruler, yardstick, meter stick, or measuring tape has repeated equal units. Centimeters and inches suit many small objects; feet and meters suit many larger distances. An adult can point to the unit label before the child reads any numbers.

Place one end at the zero mark, not automatically at the ruler’s outer edge. Read the mark reached by the other end. The spaces between marks count the length; the marks themselves show boundaries. A strip from 0 cm to 6 cm covers six one-centimeter spaces, even though seven labeled boundaries may be seen.

If the start is not zero, count the unit spaces from the start to the end or subtract the two readings. Keep the unit in the answer. A flexible tape helps along a curved edge, while a straight ruler is suitable for a straight pencil. Never assume an unmarked picture is drawn to actual size.

examples.prompt: A paper strip starts at the 0 cm mark and ends at 9 cm. What is its length?
steps: The starting boundary is zero.
Count the nine one-centimeter spaces to the endpoint.
Report nine centimeters, including the unit.

examples.prompt: A ribbon lies from 3 inches to 10 inches on a ruler. How long is it?
steps: The ribbon does not begin at zero.
Find the covered distance: 10 − 3 = 7.
Seven one-inch spaces lie between the endpoints.

weeks.title: Choose a unit and estimate length
weeks.objective: Explain how unit size affects measurement count and use known benchmarks.

connection.before: Length is counted in equal spaces from a starting point.
connection.after: Measured lengths can be compared by subtraction.

days: Cover one model length with large and small units.
Use supplied benchmarks for sensible estimates.
Practice unit-size reasoning on A.
Discuss estimates and measurement differences on B.
Defend a practical measurement comparison on C.
explanation: The same object can have different measurement numbers when the units differ. A longer unit covers more of the object at once, so fewer of those units are needed. A shorter unit covers less at once, so more are needed. The object itself has not grown or shrunk.

Use a familiar length as a benchmark before measuring. A centimeter is a small unit, while a meter is much longer; an inch is smaller than a foot. An inch is longer than a centimeter, so ten inches is longer than ten centimeters. An adult can show a labeled example of each. Estimate by imagining repeated benchmarks, then compare the estimate with an actual reading or the supplied measurement.

Estimates need not be exact, but they must be sensible for the object and stated unit. If a strip is described as about three 10 cm cards placed end to end, about 30 cm is reasonable. This week supplies benchmark sizes where calculations are needed; do not silently treat an inch and a centimeter as equal.

examples.prompt: A ribbon is covered exactly by 12 short units or 6 long units. Which unit is longer?
examples.answer: The long unit, twice the short unit.
steps: The ribbon is the same length in both measurements.
Six long units cover what twelve short units cover.
Each long unit replaces two short ones, so fewer are needed.

examples.prompt: A shelf is about four 20 cm blocks long. Estimate its length.
steps: Each benchmark block is twenty centimeters long.
Combine four equal lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 20.
The estimate is about eighty centimeters, not an exact measurement.

items.prompt: Choose the sensible estimate for a pencil: 15 cm or 15 m.

items.skill: Explain how unit size affects measurement count and use known benchmarks.

items.prompt: A ribbon needs 8 short units. Each long unit is as long as 2 short units. How many long units cover it?

Four pairs correspond to four long units.
items.skill: Explain how unit size affects measurement count and use known benchmarks.

items.prompt: A bench is about three 1-foot tiles long. Estimate its length.

items.skill: Explain how unit size affects measurement count and use known benchmarks.

steps: Small units cover less distance each.

items.prompt: For a room’s width, why might meters be easier than centimeters?

items.prompt: A strip measures 10 centimeters and a second strip measures 10 inches. Which is longer?
steps: An inch is longer than a centimeter.

items.skill: Explain how unit size affects measurement count and use known benchmarks.

items.prompt: Describe a fair way to compare two children’s length measurements when they used different units.
items.answer: Sample: measure both lengths again using the same unit.
steps: Different unit sizes can produce different counts for the same length.
Using one common unit lets the numbers be compared directly.

weeks.title: Compare and combine measured lengths
weeks.objective: Solve addition and subtraction length stories within one hundred.

connection.before: Measurements need a number and a unit.
connection.after: Number lines will show these distances as moves.

days: Align strip drawings at a shared start.
Label joined, removed, and missing lengths.
Solve single length relationships on A.
Explain overlaps and unit errors on B.
Complete two-step measurement stories on C.
explanation: Lay two imagined strips at the same starting point. The extra part of the longer strip is the difference in their lengths. For 18 cm and 11 cm, the unmatched part is 7 cm. Subtract lengths only after making sure the measurements use the same unit.

Joining strips end to end with no overlap adds their lengths. Cutting off a piece subtracts its length. In a two-step problem, label the length after the first action before applying the second. The physical action helps a child choose an operation without relying on a single word.

Draw simple bars and label every known length. A missing section plus a known section must equal the whole. Check a cut by adding the removed piece back, or check a comparison by adding the difference to the shorter length. Our story lengths and totals remain within one hundred.

examples.prompt: A green strip is 42 cm long; a yellow strip is 27 cm long. How much longer is the green strip?
steps: Start both strips at the same point in a drawing.
Subtract the shorter length: 42 − 27 = 15.
Check that 27 + 15 = 42 centimeters.

examples.prompt: A cord is 35 inches long. Add 18 inches, then cut off 12 inches. Find its final length.
steps: Joining gives 35 + 18 = 53 inches.
Cutting removes length: 53 − 12 = 41.
The final answer still uses inches.

weeks.title: Show operations as number-line moves
weeks.objective: Represent whole numbers and operations on equally spaced number lines.

connection.before: Differences count distance between measurements.
connection.after: Line plots will place data above number-line positions.

days: Draw and label equal number-line spaces.
Use arrows for positive additions and removals.
Read starts and endpoints on A.
Distinguish distances from marks on B.
Connect measurement stories to routes on C.
explanation: A number line uses equally spaced marks for equal-sized steps. Begin by deciding what one space represents. If labels are 0, 10, 20, 30 at neighboring marks, each space is ten; if they are 0, 1, 2, 3, each space is one. A number’s location describes its distance from zero.

Addition moves right by the amount being added. Subtraction can move left by the amount removed. Start at the first number rather than always at zero when showing a calculation. To show 26 + 14, begin at 26, move ten to 36, then four to 40. Label the start, moves, and endpoint.

A difference can also be the distance counted upward from the smaller number to the larger. Both models are useful, but explain what the answer labels: an endpoint after removing, or a gap between two points. Count the spaces crossed, not the number of labeled marks visited.

examples.prompt: Show 34 + 23 with a +20 jump and a +3 jump.
steps: Start at 34 because it is the first addend.
Move twenty right to 54.
Move three more right to 57.

examples.prompt: Show 62 − 18 with a leftward jump of 10 then 8.
steps: Begin at 62.
Remove ten by moving left to 52.
Remove the remaining eight by moving left to 44.

steps: Moving left removes nine.

steps: The starting point is twenty.

steps: 50 − 40 confirms the same spacing.

worksheets.directions: An adult may read the directions aloud. Use counters, bundles, drawings, or a number line when helpful. Explain your thinking aloud or in writing; include units when needed.

steps: Addition increases a positive whole-number amount.

weeks.title: Record whole-unit lengths on line plots
weeks.objective: Organize supplied whole-unit measurements and interpret each mark.

connection.before: A number line places equal units in order.
connection.after: Other kinds of data will use category graphs.

days: Place one counter per measurement above a number line.
Replace counters with X marks and write a key.
Read and create simple plots on A.
Separate object counts from length labels on B.
Audit a measurement plot using C.
explanation: A line plot places one mark above a number for each measured object with that length. If three strips are 4 cm long, stack three X marks above 4. The number labels describe lengths; the X marks count objects. An adult can cross off each measurement after plotting it so none are omitted or counted twice.

Include every whole-unit label from the smallest measurement to the largest, even if some have no X marks. Keep those labels equally spaced and label the unit. A key such as one X means one strip explains what each mark counts. The total number of X marks should equal the number of measurements.

To find the most common length, look for the tallest stack. To compare the longest and shortest lengths, subtract the number-line labels, not the stack heights. To find how many objects have two selected lengths, add the counts above those labels. Read the question carefully to know whether it asks for objects or centimeters.

examples.prompt: Plot these strip lengths in centimeters: 3, 4, 4, 6, 3, 4. Describe every stack from 3 through 6.
examples.answer: 3 cm: XX; 4 cm: XXX; 5 cm: none; 6 cm: X. One X means one strip.
steps: Sort the list into two threes, three fours, zero fives, and one six.
Place those counts above equally spaced labels 3, 4, 5, 6.
The stacks contain six X marks, matching six strips.

examples.prompt: A line plot has 5 cm: XX, 6 cm: X, 7 cm: XXX; one X is one stick. How many sticks and how much longer is the longest than the shortest?
steps: Count marks: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 sticks.
Read the extreme measured lengths as 5 cm and 7 cm.
Subtract 7 − 5 = 2 cm; stack counts are not lengths.

items.prompt: A plot has 1 cm: X, 2 cm: XXX, 3 cm: XX. How many objects are measured?
steps: Count one, three, and two marks.

items.prompt: A plot has 4 in: X, 5 in: XXXX, 6 in: XX. Which length is most common?
steps: Five inches has four marks.
That stack is taller than the stacks of one and two marks.
items.skill: Organize supplied whole-unit measurements and interpret each mark.

days: Sort counters by categories and name the groups.

explanation: A category graph groups objects by a name rather than a measured number. A picture graph may use one star for one vote; a bar graph may use one square of height for one object. weeks.title: Pair objects to explain odd and even
weeks.objective: Determine odd or even for collections through twenty and write doubles for even totals.

connection.before: Doubles join two equal-sized parts.
connection.after: Equal rows will organize arrays.

days: Pair actual or drawn counters with an adult.
Rearrange even totals into equal rows.
Record pairs and doubles on A.

explanation: Give each counter a partner. A collection is even when every counter belongs to a pair and none is left over. A collection is odd when exactly one counter remains without a partner. Start with actual or drawn counters rather than deciding from the last digit alone; our collections stay at twenty or fewer.

An even group can also be divided into two equal rows. Twelve counters can make two rows of six, so 12 = 6 + 6. The matching rows give an addition equation with equal addends. An odd group cannot make two equal whole-counter rows unless one counter is left outside them.

Adding one counter changes an even collection to odd because that new counter has no partner. Adding another counter makes a pair and returns to even. Encourage the child to explain the leftover or the equal rows. Avoid saying an odd collection has no pairs; it can have many pairs and still one unpaired object.

explanation: An array arranges objects in equal rows and equal columns. Rows go across and columns go up and down. A drawing with three rows of four counters has twelve counters, and each column also has the same number. An adult can guide a finger across one row, then down one column.

Write one addend for each row. Three rows of four give 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The number of addends counts rows; the size of each addend counts objects per row. This week uses at most five rows and five columns, and repeated addition rather than requiring multiplication facts.

You may also count by columns or split an array into smaller row groups. Both methods must include every object exactly once. Unequal rows are not a full rectangular array. If a row is missing a counter, show where it belongs before using an equal-row count.

explanation: A rectangle can be partitioned into rows and columns of equal-sized squares. The squares cover the whole inside without gaps or overlaps. Count the squares inside the rectangle, not just the marks on its boundary. A rectangle with two rows and three columns contains six squares.

To draw a small grid, an adult may provide square paper or help mark equal spacings. A row of three squares needs four vertical boundary lines, including the two outside edges. The number of inside dividing lines is one less than the number of rows or columns being formed.

Count by repeated addition, and check using the other direction. Three rows of four squares give 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, while four columns of three give 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. The two counts describe the same covering; no area formula or multiplication notation is required this week.

days: Trace and count flat-shape boundaries.

explanation: Look at the attributes that define a shape rather than its color, size, or direction. A triangle is a closed flat shape with three straight sides and three corners. A quadrilateral has four straight sides, a pentagon five, and a hexagon six. Count all the way around once, starting at a marked corner.

A square and a rectangle are both quadrilaterals. Turning a shape does not change its number of sides. A closed figure with curved edges is not a polygon made only of straight sides. When drawing from a description, check the side count and make sure the final side connects back to the start.

A cube is a solid shape, not a flat square. It has six square faces, twelve edges, and eight vertices, or corners. An adult can point to these features on a box-shaped model. Count each face, edge, or vertex only once; hidden parts still belong to the solid even if a drawing cannot show them all.

weeks.title: Share circles and rectangles equally
weeks.objective: Partition circles and rectangles into equal halves and thirds.

connection.before: A whole shape can be divided into nonoverlapping parts.

days: Fold or describe equal halves with an adult.

Name supplied equal shares on A.

explanation: Equal sharing means each part contains the same amount of the whole. Two equal parts are halves, and three equal parts are thirds. Count how many equal parts make the entire original shape before naming a share. Simply drawing two or three regions does not prove they are equal.

For a rectangle, equally wide strips of the same height make equal shares. For a circle, a straight cut through the center makes two equal halves. Three equal circle shares can be shown as three equal-sized wedges meeting at the center; an adult can help draw or fold a model rather than expecting precise angles.

Use the language one half, two halves, one third, and three thirds. Two halves make one whole, and three thirds make one whole. Keep the original whole the same when comparing shares. A half of a large rectangle can be larger than a half of a small rectangle, so the share name alone does not fix an amount.

explanation: Four equal shares are fourths, also called quarters. A rectangle can be divided into four equal strips or into a two-by-two grid of equal rectangles. A circle can be divided by two crossing lines through its center that make four equal wedges. Four fourths always compose the original whole.

Equal shares need equal amounts, but they do not always need identical outlines. In two identical rectangles made of eight equal square cells in two rows, a whole row of four cells can be half of one rectangle while a two-by-two block can be half of the other. Each copy must still be fully divided into two nonoverlapping parts of four cells each. Count equal squares to support the area comparison.

Have the child name the whole before naming a part. For the same whole, one fourth is smaller than one half because four fair shares divide it more finely than two. Do not compare only the height or outline of pieces. Use equal-square counts, folding, or another clear equal-area argument.

explanation: A supply plan starts with a question about quantities: what is available, what is used, or what is still needed. An adult can help the child draw one bar for the available whole and smaller labeled parts for changes. Compute the intermediate quantity before answering the final question. Two-step story quantities here stay within one hundred.

Use place-value drawings for the separate larger inventory calculations. A drawing with hundreds, tens, and ones makes trades visible; adding or removing a bundle of ten changes the value by ten, not one. Check a large addition by subtracting an addend, or check a subtraction by restoring the removed amount.

A written plan should name what every answer counts. Seventy-two pencils and seventy-two boxes are different claims. Ask the child to explain why the chosen operations match the actions, then compare a second method. Choosing a convenient pair of addends can simplify the work without changing the supply total.

weeks.title: Explain, check, and present a design
weeks.objective: Create a coherent report using operations, measurement, arrays, and data.

connection.before: A model, an equation, and a unit together support a claim.
connection.after: Grade 3 extends equal rows into multiplication and numbered fraction work.

days: Review what makes a report reproducible.
Choose models matched to the question.
Rehearse calculations and checks on A.
Revise flawed reports on B.
Present a complete design explanation using C.
explanation: A final design report should be understandable to someone who did not watch the work. State the goal, list the supplied amounts, show a drawing or written model, and answer the question with a unit. An adult may write the child’s spoken explanation while the child points to the quantities and checks their meanings.

Choose a representation because it fits the problem. Equal rows show seating or square spaces; number-line jumps show changes or distances; a graph organizes category counts or measured lengths. Two-step stories need a labeled intermediate result. Large inventory computations should still show hundreds, tens, and ones rather than unexplained digit rules.

Finish with evidence that could catch a mistake. Add back what was removed, count an array in both directions, check graph marks against its source list, or compare an estimate with a measurement. A correct final number with an unclear explanation should be revised so a partner can follow and reproduce the reasoning.

examples.prompt: A display has 4 rows of 4 spaces. There are 7 drawings and 6 captions, one item per space. How many spaces remain? Give a model and check.
steps: Capacity is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.
Used spaces total 7 + 6 = 13, leaving 16 − 13 = 3.
Check that seven drawings, six captions, and three blanks fill all sixteen.

examples.prompt: A report says strip lengths 5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 5 cm give six strips and most common length 5 cm. Verify both claims.
steps: Count six measurements in the list.
Group them: 5 cm has three, 6 cm has two, 7 cm has one.
The counts total six and the tallest stack belongs to five centimeters.
